passage:
Hi Simran,
Quick update on our history project. I asked the chatbot for sources on old trade routes and it gave me three book titles with authors and page numbers, all very confident. Yesterday I went to the school library to borrow them. Two of them don't exist, and the third is about something else. I felt silly, like I'd been lied to by someone friendly.
The librarian showed me how to search the catalogue, and we found one real book that fits. So I'm rewriting the bibliography from things I can actually hold in my hand. Could you check the dates in my section against your notes?
Thanks, Maria 🙂

qa.q: How many of the three book titles turned out not to exist?
How did Maria feel after discovering the titles were fake?
qa.a: Maria felt silly, as if lied to by someone friendly.

qa.q: What can Maria do with any chatbot answer that comes with sources?
qa.a: Maria can cross-check with books, teachers or reliable sites, using the library catalogue to see that a source exists before relying on it.

qa.q: How might the librarian see Maria's problem?
qa.a: The librarian probably sees a common mistake, since they showed Maria how to search the catalogue and helped find a real book instead of scolding.

grounding: Shows a teen finding that a confident chatbot invented sources and cross-checking with the library.

passage:
Subject: My history project sources

Dear Mr Yusuf,

I need to tell you something before you mark my project on the 1857 revolt.

I used an AI chatbot to help me find sources. It gave me five book titles with authors and page numbers. It sounded completely sure. I put them in my bibliography.

Yesterday I went to the city library to borrow one of them, and the librarian couldn't find it. Then she checked the other four. Three of them don't exist. The authors are real historians, but those books aren't theirs. The chatbot made them up.

I felt stupid and scared. I've now replaced them with two real books from the library and one article our textbook recommends, and I've checked every quote against the actual pages. The corrected version is attached.

I'm sorry. I didn't know it could invent things so confidently. I'll always cross-check now.

Regards,
Manoj, 10B

qa.q: How many of the five book titles turned out not to exist?
qa.a: Three of them don't exist, as the librarian found when she checked the other four.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling after the librarian's check?
qa.a: Manoj felt stupid and scared, worried about submitting sources the chatbot had made up.

qa.q: What did Manoj do that was wise after discovering the problem?
qa.a: Manoj replaced the fake sources with real library books and a recommended article, checked every quote and told Mr Yusuf honestly.

qa.q: How might Mr Yusuf feel reading this email?
qa.a: Mr Yusuf would likely appreciate the honesty and be glad Manoj learned to cross-check AI answers. 👍

grounding: It shows a teen misled by a chatbot that invented sources confidently, recognising that AI can sound sure and be wrong, and cross-checking with books and teachers.

passage:
So you want me to tell the class the chatbot story? Okay. I'm Farida.

Before the chemistry unit test, I asked an AI to explain which gas is released when you put zinc in dilute acid. It said oxygen. It explained it so neatly, with a little equation, that I didn't question it. I wrote "oxygen" in my notes in big letters.

The next day, at lunch, Indu was revising from the textbook. I said, "Easy, it's oxygen." She frowned. "It's hydrogen. Look." She pointed at the page and the diagram, the gas making a pop sound near a flame.

My face went hot. I'd trusted something just because it sounded sure.

So now I have a rule. If I use the chatbot, I check it against the textbook or ask Ma'am. Every time. It's still useful. It explains things well. But sounding confident and being right aren't the same.

Indu still teases me about it. "Oxygen, Farida?" Fair enough.

qa.q: Which gas did the AI wrongly say was released?
What was Farida feeling when Indu showed the right answer?
qa.a: Farida felt embarrassed, with a hot face, at having trusted the AI just because it sounded sure.

qa.q: What rule did Farida make, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Farida now checks the chatbot against the textbook or asks Ma'am every time, because AI can sound confident and still be wrong.

qa.q: How might Indu see Farida's mistake now?
qa.a: Indu seems to find it funny and teases Farida gently, without being unkind.

grounding: It shows a teen misled by a chatbot that answered confidently but wrongly, learning that AI can sound sure and be mistaken and cross-checking with books and teachers.
